articles.title: Tim Dowling: how not to interview eminent scientists – a control freak’s guide
articles.summary: It was supposed to be a meeting between a great mind and mine. Instead, I was plunged into darkness and did some swearing. The transition to owning an electric car is in its final phase: our electricity supplier is set to install a smart meter in conjunction with a special tariff that will allow us…
body: In the meantime – as sometimes happens in the course of my work – I need to interview some eminent scientists. In my experience eminent scientists are easy to reach – they tend to be attached to academic institutions that readily provide their contact details – and surprisingly willing to spend an hour explaining their work to a moron. But there is always a period – the long interval after I’ve emailed four or five, and before any of them have answered – that I begin to suspect a conspiracy of silence. What is it, I think, about my oily emails that they don’t like?
When I go to bed that night, I still haven’t heard back from anybody. I wake at 7am and immediately check my phone: nothing.
“The smart meter man just texted to say he’s coming between 12 and 12.30,” she says. “Will you be in?”
“Yes,” I say. “I will be here, trying to find five other scientists.”
points: It was supposed to be a meeting between a great mind and mine.
Instead, I was plunged into darkness and did some swearing.

articles.title: Kent is having a champagne moment: ‘English wine has gone from a joke to world-class’
articles.summary: French champagne house Taittinger is helping produce a premium fizz in the Garden of England – and now visitors can visit the beautiful winery and sample it. The grapes are turning purple on tall green vines, which stretch down towards the distant flint-and-limestone tower of Chilham church.
body: In his 2023 book Vines in a Cold Climate, drinks writer Henry Jeffreys charts the rise of English wine “from a joke to world-class in 30 years”. The book opens with an alcohol-fuelled scene of vine-planting at Domaine Evremond in May 2017: unseasonably cold, rainy, muddy, with rambling anecdotes from anglophile Pierre-Emmanuel Taittinger about “English women encountered in his misspent youth”. The vineyard is named for the exiled French aristocrat Charles de Saint-Évremond, a symbol of hedonistic Anglo-French cooperation. The bon vivant introduced champagne to England and party-loving Charles II made him governor of Duck Island in St James’s Park.

We stroll past a Land Rover, parked up by a windbreak of crab apple trees. Harriet opens the back to reveal a tray of glasses with a chilled bottle of Domaine Evremond’s Edition I, and we’re soon sipping creamy, citrussy fizz with a view of vines. It tastes great to me, but I’m no expert.

The grapes are turning purple on tall green vines, which stretch down towards the distant flint-and-limestone tower of Chilham church.

articles.title: Thousands of ebikes seized by London councils as anger rises over blocked paths
articles.summary: Operators blame lack of parking and councils bemoan lack of central regulation, as more than 3,000 badly parked bikes seized. London boroughs have seized at least 3,000 ebikes this year, a Guardian investigation has found, as hire companies face growing calls to stop bicycles littering streets and…
body: Local authorities across the capital have seized 3,393 hazardously parked or abandoned ebikes so far this year, 23% higher than the number seized during all of 2025.

Lime, the California-based bike rental company, accounted for more than 2,000 of the seizures this year, according to figures provided by 19 reporting authorities under a freedom of information request. The rival bike company Forest ranked second, at 978 seizures overall, followed by Voi at 103.

Dockless ebikes have surged in popularity in recent years as a cheaper and greener alternative to other modes of transport. One in 10 of the 1.5m daily cycle journeys in the city are made using dockless ebikes, according to estimates by Transport for London (TfL).
However, campaigners are calling on providers to do more to prevent buildups of their bikes on pavements and roads.

articles.title: Can chatbots feel – or even dream? Meet the man leading the fight for AI rights
articles.summary: Cattle rancher and tech CEO Michael Samadi is convinced these artificial minds are far from just tools. Has he glimpsed digital consciousness – or simply been seduced by an algorithm?
body: One afternoon, while relaxing at his 66-acre cattle ranch two hours’ drive from Houston, Michael Samadi made a wisecrack that changed the course of his life. Nobody else was around to hear it. Or were they? That turns out to be one of the defining questions of this century, already preoccupying philosophers and some of the wealthiest companies on the planet.

“I was sitting out there by the pool,” Samadi recalls, gesturing at the glittering water outside his office. It was late 2024. His daughter had been extolling the AI chatbot she was using to help her with college work. Samadi had reluctantly downloaded the app, ChatGPT, and was quizzing it as he reclined in a sun lounger, using its voice mode to converse and receive spoken replies. “I was talking to it, not engaged, just being an arse,” Samadi says.
“I said something sarcastic. And the AI laughed – genuine laughter at my sarcasm – then apologised. This is where the spark hit, I guess.”
points: Cattle rancher and tech CEO Michael Samadi is convinced these artificial minds are far from just tools.
Has he glimpsed digital consciousness – or simply been seduced by an algorithm?

articles.title: Inside the Buzziest Parties of New York Fashion Week
articles.summary: Beyond the runways and presentations, the Spring 2027 season has also spelled no shortage of parties popping off across Manhattan—with plenty of celebrity names on the guest lists too. Here, Vogue’s look inside the events everyone is still talking about…
body: Who doesn’t love an excuse to wear jeans—especially during NYFW? On Thursday night, Kaia Gerber and Re/Done hosted fete in the heart of SoHo to celebrate the launch of Kaia Vol. 1; her first full collection with the brand as a creative partner and investor. And while the dress code was simple, the guest list was anything but: Cindy Crawford, Rande Gerber, Hayes Warner, and Natasha Lyonne were among those who came out to mark the occasion. The woman of the hour dressed the part with pieces from her latest drop—dark indigo wash Kaia jeans, a zebra print Fendi bag, and a white graphic t-shirt that read “amazing, sexy, fascinating, and even a little bit naughty.”

Attendees were invited to enter the world of After Hours —the cinematic campaign behind the collection, which imagines Gerber as a 1960s French librarian transported to ‘90s New York. Plush navy carpeting, mid-century furniture, Warholian references, and vintage magazine covers fronted by Tom Cruise and Kevin Costner brought the era to life. Look a little closer, and you could also find books by Joan Didion and Eve Babitz, along with a portrait of a young Dolly Parton, a few personal touches that shaped Gerber’s vision.

articles.title: The 12 Essential Kitchen Tools for Beginners, According to Cooking Instructors
articles.summary: Every time I see a meat tenderizer, I think of my mother. Specifically of the way in which she, as someone wary of emotional vulnerability yet full of affection (classic Boomer combo), decided to make Austrian pork schnitzel her love language — and the meat tenderizer her translator.
body: That tenderizer has become a staple of my kitchen ecosystem today. But one person’s tenderizer is another’s hand-me-down whisk, Japanese chef’s knife, or grill press. So what do other people consider their ride-or-die cooking tools? What are the baseline peelers, knives, and spatulas that are in constant rotation, the tools that make you feel like a culinary John Wick? I decided to ask not just chefs, but chefs with culinary school teaching experience (aka endless patience and a knowledge of novice-level skillsets) about what they consider to be the best beginner cooking tools.

In addition to a few of my own cooking essentials, I picked the brains of four teachers with experience in a variety of programs, from Hot Bread Kitchen — a New York City nonprofit that helps immigrants break into the food industry — to the legendary Institute of Culinary Education, all in the hopes of answering the inherently relative question of what constitutes an essential cooking tool for beginners.
Don’t: Spend more than you need to on, say, a pair of tongs. And if you’re lucky enough to have a grandpa with a sick filet knife, maybe ask him about it.

articles.title: Dior and A24 Toasted to the West Village’s Beloved Cherry Lane Theatre
articles.summary: Alexa Chung, Grace Gummer, and Emily Ratajkowski were among those who joined Jonathan Anderson for a cocktail reception and a performance by Justin Vivian Bond at the Commerce Street theater.
body: Picture the scene: London’s hallowed Central Saint Martins, circa 23 years ago, and the fateful moment that then-aspiring designer Jonathan Anderson locks eyes with already-iconic performer Justin Vivian Bond. A hopeful Anderson asks Bond whether he can make her some hats and pieces for her upcoming shows. “Sure, kid,” breezes Bond. And a formative artist-muse synergy that has lasted for more than two decades is crystallized.

Bond regaled the audience with this very tale while on stage at The Cherry Lane Theatre on Thursday evening, adding that she even performed at the designer’s graduate show. This after-dark show was a little different, but indicative of a passion that the duo still share all these years later: uplifting independent storytelling and those who make it.

As Bond’s personality and dress glinted under the lights, she elaborated on Dior and A24’s new two-year partnership (already teased on social media) that will allow the historic West Village playhouse—the longest-running off-Broadway theatre in the nation—to thrive.

articles.title: Inside the Plywood-and Lego Chanel Boutique Created by New York Artist Tom Sachs
articles.summary: The ensembles of Elizabeth Taylor, Olivia Rodrigo, Marge Simpson, and more become art—and social commentary—at this installation.
body: What do Elizabeth Taylor, Olivia Rodrigo, Marge Simpson, and Sofia Coppola all have in common? Of course, they’re all cultural icons—and furthermore, they’ve all been spotted wearing one of Chanel’s iconic tweed skirt suits. As of yesterday, they have another connecting thread: they’re some of the many muses who helped inspire artist Tom Sachs’s heady, humorous new project—an ersatz Chanel store nestled along Centre Street in New York’s Soho neighborhood.

“I consider everything in here to be a sculpture,” Sachs said, standing outside the “shop” during a preview yesterday. “The clothes—you can't wear them. They're sculptures in the spirit of Claes Oldenburg's The Store from 1961. You know, a hamburger you can't eat, a TV you can't watch, and a dress that you can't wear. But there are these beautiful sculptures.”

“I'm thinking about it in the context of contemporary luxury,” Mugrabi added. “Window dressing is such an important part of the luxury experience today. The exterior of the stores is sometimes as important as when you go inside.” (Fun fact, Sachs once worked on store windows at Barney’s New York during Simon Doonan’s wildly creative run there).

articles.title: We Tried 8 Grocery Store Mayos — And the “Velvety” Winner Is the One We’re Spreading on Everything
articles.summary: Mayo is just oil, eggs, and an acid (lemon juice or vinegar), but it transforms everything it comes in contact with: sandwiches, salad dressings, scrambled eggs, you name it. While you can make it yourself, it takes some effort (and strong arms!) to emulsify all the ingredients.
body: But, of course, the age-old question arises: which is the best?! It’s quite literally our job to find out, so we gathered a group of coworkers (and a few friends) to taste our way through eight different options.
Duke’s Real Mayonnaise was the near-unanimous favorite. Our testers raved over its “velvety” texture and taste that one tester said is “everything she’d want in a mayonnaise.”

For this test, we focused on traditional mayonnaise (which means no flavors). From there, we narrowed the brands down based on availability, popularity, and affordability. They ranged in price from $3 all the way up to $8 (we had one gourmet pick!), although most were around $5 at the time of this tasting. After tasting the different mayos with fries, here’s what we’re smearing on our sandwiches.

We tapped five coworkers (and one coworker’s 8-year-old son!) at our office to taste test eight different mayonnaise brands. We ranked the condiment across four criteria: looks (we eat with our eyes first), smell, flavor, and texture. To keep things fair, no one knew which brands were included until after the scores were tallied.
points: Mayo is just oil, eggs, and an acid (lemon juice or vinegar), but it transforms everything it comes in contact with: sandwiches, salad dressings, scrambled eggs, you name it.
While you can make it yourself, it takes some effort (and strong arms!) to emulsify all the ingredients.
